catalog_quote: Stress is predictable for about 95% of the lexicon. For two syllable words, the default stress pattern is: (C)V́.CV: <mé.ndi> ‘boy’ ... A heavy syllable tends to pull stress to it, so CV.CV́V is stressed on the second syllable. Very few words have more than one complex vowel sequence, but when they do, the first syllable usually receives the stress, as <féa.fea> ‘Comb-crested Jacana (Iredipara gallinacea)’ below illustrates. <ga.ndáu> ‘gecko’ <sa.búa> ‘slave, follower clan’ ... <sió.sa> ‘bad, evil’ ... Three and four syllable word stems exemplify the stress pattern of an iamb. Stress is consistently assigned to the second syllable: CV.CV́.CV. ... <a.rí.ri> ‘girl’ <e.vé.tu> ‘woman’ <e.vé.ve.tu> ‘women (married)’ ... Words of four syllables and more exhibit primary and secondary stress. A few nouns fit this description; many inflected verbs do also. <a.yó.bo.rò> ‘White-tailed Rat’ <bu.bú.bu.gù.tu.rè.re> ‘we arrived a while ago, DP’ <ni.nì.ngi.gu.tá.re> ‘we heard about that (yesterday/a few days ago)’ Examples of three and four syllable words with heavy syllables include: <koá.da.va> ‘barracuda’ <ka.vái.go> ‘trouble, bad luck!’ <a.kúa.go> ‘bad’ <táu.ba.na> ‘good’ ... There are several (C)V.CV́ words in Tafota Baruga. Some are even minimal pairs with those having the default stress pattern: (C)V́.CV. <a.gha> ‘coconut shell cup’ <a.ghá> ‘thus, that way’

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is largely predictable: disyllables are stressed on the first syllable, three- and four-syllable stems on the second syllable (iambic), but a heavy syllable (complex vowel nucleus CVV or long/geminate vowel, geminates counting heavier) attracts stress (e.g. ga.ndáu, táu.ba.na, a.kúa.go); stress is fixed on the stem before intensifier, diminutive -ko and comparative -go suffixes; about 5% of the lexicon is lexically exceptional (final-stressed disyllables, many of them functors, and some initial-stressed trisyllables), with minimal pairs such as a.gha 'cup' vs a.ghá 'thus'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words of four or more syllables carry primary and secondary stress (secondary shown with grave in the section, e.g. a.yó.bo.rò, ta.tá.fu.gè, bu.bú.bu.gù.tu.rè.re); in compounds primary stress falls on the initial syllable of the first constituent and secondary on the initial syllable of the second (p. 13), though jója-tófo 'immense' has primary on both.
new_statements.exceptions: ~5% of lexicon: (C)V.CV́ disyllables (a.mó 'I', ko.tú 'and', fi.rí 'flesh', go.só 'cloud', tu.mbó 'yesterday' etc.), minimal pairs a.gha/a.ghá, e.gha/e.ghá, u.va/u.vá, u.ndu/u.ndú, bu.rú.ru ea/bú.ru.ru ea; trisyllables not following CV.CV́.CV or the heavy-syllable rule (nó.mo.no 'cross-cousin', ná.ma.ne 'we.EXC', vai.kí.na); words with two complex nuclei stress the first (féa.fea). Exceptional stress is written with an acute in the practical orthography (p. 13).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (lexical items and inflected verbs in citation form, syllabified orthographic representations); stress assignment precedes certain suffixes; vowel length and nasality are phonemic; no tone reported for Tafota Baruga. Smallhorn 2011:79-80 summarises the same facts second-hand as 'phonemic stress with a low functional load' and default penultimate stress in 2-3-syllable non-verbs.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes the Tafota dialect of Baruga (villages Erika, Foru 1, Foru 2, Guruguru; 798 speakers), one of three Baruga dialects (Bareji, Mado, Tafota; Smallhorn 2011 sec. 2.12 also treats Doghoro [dgx] as essentially a Baruga dialect). Glottolog language-level code baru1269 / ISO bjz covers all three; no separate glottocode for Tafota was checked.

new_statements.relation_note: Same volume (and same text) as the existing statement; adds the iambic second-syllable rule for 3-4-syllable stems, secondary stress in longer words and compounds, and the stem-before-suffix ordering, none of which the catalog rule (empty) or the existing statement snippet records. The volume record itself (23688) is not online; only its 15 chapter PDFs are, and only the Baruga chapter concerns this language.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress is initial in disyllables and on the second syllable in three- and four-syllable stems (an iambic (C)V.CV́.CV pattern); heavy syllables (vowel clusters, long vowels) attract stress, long vowels outranking vowel clusters; words of four or more syllables carry secondary stress (alternating, e.g. a.yó.bo.rò); stress is assigned to the stem before intensifiers and the suffixes -ko, -go are added. Compounds: primary stress on the first syllable of the first member, secondary on the first syllable of the second (p. 13).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: words of four syllables and more show primary plus secondary stress (a.yó.bo.rò 'White-tailed Rat'; bu.bú.bu.gù.tu.rè.re; ni.nì.ngi.gu.tá.re); in compounds secondary stress on the initial syllable of the second constituent (áiro-àiro, méne-mène), jója-tófo with two primaries (p. 13).
new_statements.exceptions: About 5% of the lexicon: (C)V.CV́ words incl. minimal pairs (a.gha 'cup' vs a.ghá 'thus'; u.va 'arrowroot-like plant' vs u.vá 'liver'), many of them functors (a.mó 'I/me', ko.tú 'and') but some nominals (fi.rí 'flesh', go.só 'cloud'); trisyllables not following CV.CV́.CV or the heavy-syllable rule (nó.mo.no 'cross-cousin', ná.ma.ne 'we.EXC', vai.kí.na); exceptional stress is written with an acute in the practical orthography (p. 13).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Tafota dialect of Baruga (bjz), spoken in Erika, Foru 1, Foru 2 and Guruguru villages, Oro Province (798 speakers at the census cited); Baruga also has Bareji and Mado dialects (Smallhorn 2011 sec. 2.12), which are not described. The catalog entry is for Tafota Baruga, so the identity matches.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable for about 95% of words: initial in disyllables ((C)V́.CV), second syllable in 3-4-syllable stems (CV.CV́.CV), but a heavy syllable (vowel cluster CVV or long vowel VV) pulls stress onto itself (CV.CV́V), with long vowels heavier than vowel clusters (p. 8: 'the syllable with the long vowel often has primary stress, so geminate vowels pattern as more heavy than heterogeneous vowel sequences'). The remaining ~5% are lexically stressed, including minimal pairs, and are marked with an acute in the orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Present in words of four or more syllables (shown with a grave accent in the section, not in the orthography), and on the second member of compounds (p. 13).
new_statements.exceptions: ~5% of the lexicon: final-stressed disyllables (a.ghá 'thus', u.vá 'liver', u.ndú 'for him/her', functors a.mó, i.ngá, a.ná, ko.tú, a.tá, ta.gó; nominals fi.rí, ra.gá, du.ró, du.rá, go.mbú, tu.mbó, go.só); trisyllabic minimal pair bu.rú.ru ea vs bú.ru.ru ea; initial-stressed trisyllables nó.mo.no, ná.ma.ne, é.ni.ma; vai.kí.na against the heavy-syllable rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Tafota dialect of Baruga (bjz), spoken in Erika, Foru 1, Foru 2 and Guruguru villages, Oro Province (798 speakers at the census cited); Baruga also has Bareji and Mado dialects (Smallhorn 2011 sec. 2.12), which are not described. The catalog entry is for Tafota Baruga, so the identity matches.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the two listed works: they are one and the same text (the Farr and Farr 2004 OPD update printed as chapter 1 of Parker's 2005 volume). The only other description held by the project, Smallhorn 2011 (Pacific Linguistics 625, pp. 79-80, PDF 95-96; not in the works list), cites Farr and Farr 2004:10 for 'phonemic stress with a low functional load' in Tafota Baruga and assumes 'penultimate stress.. for two- and three-syllable words (at least in the case of non-verbs)' across Binanderean including Tafota Baruga. That is compatible in placement for 2-3-syllable words (initial in disyllables, second syllable in trisyllables are both penultimate) but is a different framing: Farr and Farr call the pattern iambic (second syllable in 3-4-syllable stems, e.g. a.yó.bo.rò rather than penultimate), make heavy syllables override the default, and treat the minimal pairs as ~5% lexical exceptions rather than as a phonemic stress system. Farr and Farr say nothing about tone beyond the section heading; Smallhorn discusses tone/pitch accent only for Binandere, Suena and Zia.
